questions.question: Distinguish historical cost from prudence, and give the tell-tale sign of each in a scenario.
questions.expected_answer: Historical cost keeps an asset at its original, verifiable purchase price rather than today's estimated value — tell-tale sign: an asset 'now worth more' but 'still shown at' what was paid. Prudence chooses the cautious figure under uncertainty: anticipate possible losses, never record uncertain gains — tell-tale sign: a possible loss recorded now, or a hoped-for gain refused. Land kept at R650 000 is historical cost; a doubtful debt written down is prudence.

questions.question: Apply the matching principle to insurance of R24 000 paid on 1 April for twelve months when the financial year ends 30 June.
questions.expected_answer: Only the portion that served this financial period is this year's expense: three months, April to June, which is R24 000 times three twelfths, R6 000. The remaining R18 000 is a prepaid expense belonging to next year. Matching recognises expenses in the period they occur, not when the cash happened to move, so profit fairly matches this year's costs against this year's income.

questions.question: Split the three-part scenario — the revalued van, the unrecorded groceries, and the emigrated debtor — and name the principle answering each part.
questions.expected_answer: The van stays at its purchase price because the invoice is fact and the higher value is opinion — historical cost. The R950 of groceries crossed from business to owner and must be recorded as drawings — business entity rule. The emigrated customer's R1 500 debt is a hope, not an asset, and must be written off — prudence. Multi-part scenarios are split into actions, each calling its own principle.
